TITLE 
“Evaluation of Banana Peel Nano-Fertilizer for Food Crops in Lunar Regolith 
Simulant during Post-germination Growth and Substrate Nutrient Analysis.” 
 
 Introduction 
As space exploration becomes more advanced, scientists have begun exploring how plants 
could be grown beyond Earth. This is especially important for places like the Moon, where 
future missions may rely on being able to grow crops with their given conditions. The 
surface of the moon is covered in a substance called regolith, which is very different from 
Earth's soil. Regular soil contains organic matter and microorganisms that help support 
plant growth, but regolith does not, making it a much more difficult environment for plants 
to survive in. 
Due to regolith lacking biological components, it also has physical properties that can make 
plant growth more challenging. Its particles are very fine and irregular, which allows them 
to pack closely together. This can limit the ability of a plant's roots to spread and take in 
water. At the same time, the way regolith holds water is different from soil, which can 
create inconsistent growing conditions. Plants grown in regolith often do not grow as well 
as those in normal soil as a result. 
The way various fertilizers interact under low nutrient conditions is another crucial aspect 
of plant growth research. Plants may rely on organic matter and naturally occurring 
nutrients in ordinary soil systems, but in harsher or artificial environments, external nutrient

sources become far more crucial. As a result of this, when regular soil conditions are 
unavailable, researchers frequently investigate alternate fertilizers to evaluate how well 
they can promote plant health. Gaining insight into how plants react to these types of details 
can help develop better methods for producing food in settings where conventional 
agriculture is not possible. 
 Theory 
Plant growth depends on having access to key nutrients, especially nitrogen, phosphorus, 
and potassium. These nutrients support basic functions like leaf development, energy 
transfer, and overall growth. In normal soil, plants are able to get these nutrients through 
organic matter and natural processes that happen over time. When those processes are 
missing, plants have to rely much more on whatever nutrients are added from the outside. 
This becomes more noticeable in something like lunar regolith simulant. Since it does not 
contain organic matter or living organisms, it does not naturally support nutrient cycling 
the way soil does. Even if some elements are present, they are not always in forms that 
plants can easily use. As a result, plants growing in this type of environment are more likely 
to experience stress and slower growth. Studies have shown that while plants can survive 
in regolith, they often do not develop as well as they do in regular soil (Paul et al., 2022). 
Fertilizer plays a much bigger role when the growing environment is limited like this. 
Nutrients such as nitrogen help with leaf and stem growth, phosphorus is important for 
root development, and potassium helps regulate water and overall plant health. When these 
are added in the right amounts, they can improve how well a plant grows. Still, it is not 
just about how much nutrient is added, but how available it is to the plant. 
The banana peel nano fertilizer used in this study is based on that idea. Banana peels 
contain nutrients, especially potassium, and when they are processed into much smaller 
particles, those nutrients may be easier for plants to absorb. Smaller particles can move 
more easily through the root system, which may allow plants to take in nutrients more 
efficiently compared to a standard fertilizer. This is one reason why nano fertilizers are 
being looked at more closely in plant growth research (Hussein et al., 2019).

The type of plant also matters. Tomato plants usually grow faster and require more 
nutrients, especially nitrogen, to support that growth. Basil tends to grow at a slower rate 
and may respond differently when nutrient levels change. For that reason, the two plants 
may not show the same results even when they are grown under the same conditions. 
The growing environment also changes how effective a fertilizer can be. Soil is generally 
better at holding water and nutrients, which helps plants absorb what they need over time. 
Regolith simulant does not have those same properties, so nutrients may not stay available 
for as long. Even with that limitation, a fertilizer that improves nutrient uptake could still 
make a difference in how well plants grow. 
Based on this, it is expected that plants grown in soil will perform better overall than those 
grown in regolith simulant. It is also expected that the banana peel nano fertilizer will lead 
to better growth compared to the regular fertilizer, since the nutrients may be easier for 
the plants to absorb. Tomato plants are likely to show a stronger response to these changes 
than basil since they generally require more nutrients to support their growth. 
To evaluate this, plant growth can be observed through changes in height, spread, and leaf 
development. Looking at these factors makes it easier to compare how each plant responds 
under different conditions and gives a clearer picture of how both the environment and the 
fertilizer affect growth. 
 Hypotheses 
Our project investigates the growth of tomato and basil plants by comparing experimental 
groups treated with Banana Peel Nano Fertilizer (BPNF) to control groups without fertilizer, 
using both regular soil and lunar regolith simulant. If plants are grown with BPNF, then they 
will exhibit higher concentrations of essential nutrients—specifically nitrogen, potassium, 
and phosphorus—than the plants grown without the nano fertilizer. 
We expect that our plants grown in regular soil will generally show stronger growth due to 
its natural nutrient content and water retention properties. In contrast, lunar regolith 
simulant lacks organic matter, has low nutrient availability, and exhibits poor water 
retention, which limits nutrient diffusion and root support. However, the addition of BPNF 
is predicted to significantly improve plant growth in the regolith simulant. In other words, 
the BNF features will fill in for the factors that the lunar regolith lacks.

This is because BPNF enhances diffusion and fluid transport by increasing surface area at 
the nanoscale, improving water distribution, and helping retain nutrients near plant roots. 
As a result, the combination of regolith simulant and BPNF may compensate for the soil’s 
physical and chemical limitations, leading to improved nutrient uptake and overall plant 
development. The nano fertilizer will provide a greater surface area for nutrients having to 
be absorbed for the plants and their roots. We are examining this process with the mindset 
of tomato and basil plants in specific conditions different from regular soil to prosper in 
shoot growth and root nutrition. 
The addition of Banana Peel Nano Fertilizer (BPNF) will improve fluid and nutrient transport 
within plant roots. Because lunar regolith environments simulate lower gravity conditions, 
water and nutrient movement is less efficient compared to Earth soil. The use of 
nanoparticles enhances this process by increasing surface area and improving the 
dissolution and diffusion of essential nutrients. As a result, nutrients can move more 
efficiently through the soil and into the plant roots, supporting better growth despite 
reduced gravitational effects. 
- 
Halternative1: Tomato and basil plants grown in lunar regolith simulant with Banana 
Peel Nano Fertilizer will exhibit increased shoot growth compared to plants grown 
in regolith without fertilizer. 
- 
H01: The addition of Banana Peel Nano Fertilizer to lunar regolith simulant will not 
significantly affect the plant’s shoot increase in tomato and basil plants. 
- 
Ha2: Banana Peel Nano Fertilizer will enhance diffusion and fluid transport in the 
soil, resulting in higher concentrations of nitrogen, potassium, and phosphorus in 
the roots of tomato and basil plants. 
- 
H01: Banana Peel Nano Fertilizer will not significantly affect diffusion, fluid transport, 
or the concentration of nitrogen, potassium, and phosphorus compared to plants 
grown without fertilizer or in regular soil. 
 Measurement and Methods 
Experimental Design 
This study investigates whether the Banana Peel Nano Fertilizer (BNF), which has been 
shown to increase germination percentage, can promote post-germination growth in food 
crops such as tomato and basil. Two substrates were used: soil and lunar regolith simulant. 
Two fertilizer treatments were applied: regular fertilizer (RF) and BNF. RF was a customized 
fertilizer prepared with the same concentrations of nitrogen, potassium, and phosphorus 
as BNF, dissolved in laboratory-prepared reverse osmosis water. Each plant was grown in a

separate container with a total of 28 plants across 8 treatment groups arranged in a factorial 
design. To focus on the post-germination process, germination was conducted outside the 
substrates prior to transplanting, as seeds have been confirmed to germinate in lunar 
regolith within two days(NASA, 2025).

Experimental Procedure 
1. Plant preparation 
Seeds were wrapped in a moist paper towel, sealed in a ziplock bag, and left to sprout. 
Sprouted seeds were transplanted into the prepared containers after one week. 
2. Substrate preparation 
Each container was lined with a coffee filter to retain moisture and prevent rapid leaching. 
A cotton wick was inserted at the base of each container to maintain consistent moisture 
distribution throughout the substrate through capillary water movement. 
3. Fertilizer Preparation 
NPK fertilizer 
NPK refers to macronutrients most demanded by plants: nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and 
potassium (K). These nutrients are frequently deficient in natural soil, making NPK 
fertilization one of the most common approaches to improving plant growth. Unlike 
potassium, which can be released through mineral weathering, nitrogen and phosphorus 
are not replenished through atmospheric reactions and must therefore be absorbed by 
plants through the roots. Supplementing these nutrients supports plant metabolism and 
creates conditions conducive to accelerated growth.

RF（Regular Fertilizer） 
The RF used in this study was a customized laboratory-prepared NPK blended fertilizer, 
formulated by dissolving nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium at equivalent concentrations 
to BNF, dissolved in reverse osmosis water.

BNF (Banana Peel Nano Fertilizer) 
BNF leverages nanotechnology and green chemistry to extract nanoscale(19-55nm) NPK 
elements from banana peel waste. Banana peels account for approximately 18-33% of the 
total fruit mass and are widely discarded as solid waste (Hussein et al., 2019). Using BNF 
is an environmentally sustainable alternative to conventional fertilizers. BNF was prepared 
in the laboratory following the protocol described by Hussein et al. (2019). 
Fertilizer Application Schedule 
Fertilizer was applied weekly from week one to four at a consistent dosage; RF: 45ml and 
BNF 4.83g. As RF and BNF differ in forms, powder and liquid, the amounts applied varied; 
however, the concentrations were calculated to be equivalent between the two treatments.

4. Measurements 
Shoot length was measured weekly for five weeks, starting in the first week after fertilizer 
application. Canopy width and leaf count were additionally recorded in the final week. 
Substrate NPK Nutrient concentrations were determined spectrophotometrically at the end 
of the experiment. 
 Substrate Nutrient Analysis (NPK Determination) 
 
The concentrations of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K) in the experimental 
substrates (Regolith Banana Fertilizer, Soil Banana Fertilizer, Regolith Regular Fertilizer and 
Soil Regular Fertilizer) were quantified via UV–Vis spectrophotometry using a Thermo Fisher 
Spectronic 200 in combination with the LaMotte NPK Test Kit. This analysis was designed 
to evaluate the relative nutrient availability and retention capacity of each substrate under 
identical experimental conditions. 
Calibration and Standard Preparation 
Calibration curves were established for each analyte prior to sample analysis. Stock 
solutions (2000 ppm) were prepared using analytical-grade ammonium nitrate (NH₄NO₃) 
and monobasic potassium phosphate (KH₂PO₄), providing known concentrations of nitrate 
(NO₃⁻), potassium (K⁺), and phosphate (PO₄³⁻). 
Serial dilutions of the stock solutions were performed to generate a set of working standards 
spanning the expected concentration range of the samples. Absorbance measurements of 
these standards were used to construct calibration curves for each nutrient. Linear 
regression analysis was applied to determine the relationship between absorbance and 
concentration, ensuring correlation coefficients (R²) ≥ 0.99 for all analytes. 
Spectrophotometric Determination 
Absorbance measurements were conducted following the colorimetric protocols specified in 
the LaMotte test kit. The relationship between absorbance and concentration was 
interpreted according to the Beer–Lambert law: 
A=ε b c 
where A is the measured absorbance, ε is the molar absorptivity, b is the optical path length 
of the cuvette (typically 1 cm), and c is the analyte concentration. Calibration curves were 
used to convert absorbance values into concentrations expressed in ppm.

Sample Extraction and Analysis 
Substrate samples were processed according to the standardized extraction procedures 
provided by the LaMotte NPK Test Kit. Extracted solutions were filtered as required to 
remove particulates prior to analysis. 
Absorbance readings were obtained using the Spectronic 200 spectrophotometer at the 
appropriate wavelengths for each analyte, as defined by the colorimetric method. Blank 
corrections were applied using reagent controls to minimize background interference.

Quality Control and Data Reliability 
To ensure analytical accuracy and precision, the following quality control measures were 
implemented: 
 
Calibration verification using independent standards 
 
Blank subtraction to correct for reagent and solvent absorbance 
 
Monitoring of instrument stability and baseline drift 
The resulting nutrient concentrations represent estimates of bioavailable N, P, and K in each 
substrate. These data were used to assess differences in nutrient retention and release 
behavior between Regolith Banana Fertilizer, Soil Banana Fertilizer, Regolith Regular 
Fertilizer and Soil Regular Fertilizer, providing insight into their suitability for plant growth 
applications.

5. Statistical Analysis 
Statistical significance of shoot length, canopy width, and leaf count was assessed using 
one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test, performed in R (version 4.5.3).

 Analysis and Results 
Data Analysis 
Significance testing (ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD post-hoc test) 
Statistical Analysis 
For shoot length, consistent results were observed in both tomato and basil, with the largest 
average mean difference occurred between Soil (BNF) and Regolith (RF). 
For canopy width, the largest mean difference in basil also occurred between Soil (BNF) 
and Regolith (RF), while in tomato, the largest difference was observed between Soil (RF) 
and Soil (BNF) . A similar pattern was found in leaf count for both species, with the largest 
mean difference occurring between Soil (RF) and Soil (BNF). This observation suggests that 
Soil (BNF) is the most efficient growth-accelerator pair across all measured parameters. 
This is further supported by the statistical significance of the comparisons involving 
Soil(BNF), which consistently yielded the lowest p-values, indicating that the superior 
performance of Soil(BNF) was unlikely to be due to chance. 
Meanwhile, Soil (RF) and Regolith (RF) showed the lowest mean growth values across most 
parameters, indicating that laboratory prepared NPK is less effective at promoting nutrient 
uptake. This indicates BNF performs more efficient replenishment in roots. 
Overall, tomato demonstrated substantially greater growth than basil across all measured 
parameters. In addition to higher absolute values, the tomato presented smaller standard 
errors, which indicates that the tomato has a more reliable, consistent growth pattern than 
basil throughout the experiment. It is determined that tomato is more compatible with BNF 
than Basil. 
Across all results, Regolith (BNF) consistently outperformed Regolith (RF), demonstrating 
that even nutrient-poor regolith retains the potential for plant growth when supplemented 
with BNF.

treatments for both fertilizer types. The highest nitrate concentration was observed in Soil 
+ Banana Fertilizer (32.11 ppm), whereas the lowest was measured in Regolith + 
Regular Fertilizer (7.31 ppm). This pattern suggests that soil provides a more favorable 
medium for nitrogen retention than regolith.

A similar substrate-related trend was observed for phosphorus, although the regolith 
treatments yielded negative calculated values. These values are not physically meaningful 
and likely indicate concentrations below the detection limit or the presence of matrix-related 
interference. 
For potassium, both soil and regolith treatments amended with banana fertilizer showed 
substantially higher concentrations than their regular fertilizer counterparts. The highest 
potassium concentration was measured in Soil + Banana Fertilizer (171.48 ppm), 
followed by Regolith + Banana Fertilizer (152.37 ppm). In contrast, Soil + Regular 
Fertilizer and Regolith + Regular Fertilizer showed lower potassium concentrations of 
100.54 ppm and 96.80 ppm, respectively. 
Effect of Fertilizer Type 
Banana-derived fertilizer resulted in higher nitrate and potassium concentrations than 
regular fertilizer in both substrates. In soil, nitrate increased from 18.54 ppm with regular 
fertilizer to 32.11 ppm with banana fertilizer, while potassium increased from 100.54 ppm 
to 171.48 ppm. In regolith, nitrate increased from 7.31 ppm to 9.66 ppm, and potassium 
increased from 96.80 ppm to 152.37 ppm. 
These results suggest that the banana-based fertilizer may provide a greater supply of 
readily measurable nitrogen and potassium than the regular fertilizer under the tested 
conditions. 
Phosphorus Measurement Limitations 
Phosphorus measurements showed greater variability than nitrate and potassium. While 
positive phosphorus concentrations were obtained for the soil treatments, the regolith 
treatments produced negative calculated values. These results likely reflect concentrations 
below the calibration range, baseline noise, or matrix interference associated with regolith 
extracts. Therefore, phosphorus data from regolith treatments should be interpreted with 
caution.

 Discussion and Conclusions 
Enhanced Plant Growth with Banana Fertilizer 
The results of this study demonstrate that banana fertilizer (BF) promotes enhanced plant 
growth compared to regular fertilizer (RF), particularly in soil systems and, to a slighter 
extent, in regolith. This trend is supported by both plant growth observations and 
quantitative nutrient analysis. 
Specifically, nitrate concentrations were highest in Soil + BF (32.11 ppm) compared to Soil 
+ RF (18.54 ppm), while regolith treatments showed lower but consistent increases with 
BF (9.66 ppm) relative to RF (7.31 ppm). Similarly, potassium concentrations were 
substantially higher in BF treatments, reaching 171.48 ppm in soil and 152.37 ppm in 
regolith, compared to 100.54 ppm and 96.80 ppm, respectively, in RF treatments. 
These results indicate that BF enhances nutrient availability, particularly for nitrogen and 
potassium, which directly influence shoot and leaf development. Although the experimental 
duration was limited to five weeks, the observed differences suggest that BF provides a 
more effective nutrient delivery mechanism during early plant growth stages. 
Mechanisms Behind Banana Fertilizer Performance 
The superior performance of BF can be attributed to several interacting mechanisms: 
 
High potassium availability: Elevated potassium concentrations (up to 171.48 
ppm) likely contributed to improved plant physiological performance, including 
water regulation, enzyme activation, and photosynthesis. 
 
Improved nitrogen availability: Higher nitrate concentrations in BNF treatments 
(up to 32.11 ppm) suggest enhanced nitrogen supply, a critical factor in vegetative 
growth. 
 
Slow-release behavior: Unlike RF, which provides nutrients in highly soluble forms, 
BF likely releases nutrients gradually through organic matter decomposition, 
reducing leaching losses.

 
Organic matter interactions: Organic compounds in BF may increase water 
retention, enhance microbial activity, and facilitate nutrient stabilization through 
organo-mineral interactions. 
These combined effects provide a mechanistic explanation for the increased growth 
observed in BF treatments. 
Substrate Limitations and Regolith Behavior 
As hypothesized, soil outperformed regolith in terms of nutrient retention and plant growth. 
This is reflected in consistently higher nitrate concentrations in soil treatments (32.11 ppm 
vs. 9.66 ppm for BF: 18.54 ppm vs. 7.31 ppm for RF). 
The lower nutrient concentrations in regolith highlight its limited capacity to retain and 
supply nutrients, likely due to its lack of organic matter and low cation exchange capacity. 
Additionally, potassium concentrations, while elevated in BF treatments, remained slightly 
lower in regolith (152.37 ppm) compared to soil (171.48 ppm), further supporting the role 
of substrate structure in nutrient retention. 
Despite these limitations, plant growth was achieved in regolith, demonstrating that it can 
support biological systems when supplemented with appropriate fertilizers. 
Interaction Between Fertilizer Type and Substrate 
The interaction between fertilizer type and substrate is critical in determining nutrient 
availability and plant growth. BF consistently resulted in higher nitrate and potassium 
concentrations than RF across both substrates. 
A key observation was that in regolith, BF enabled early plant growth where RF did not 
produce measurable shoot growth during the initial stage of the experiment. This suggests 
that BF improves early-stage nutrient accessibility, particularly in nutrient-poor substrates. 
However, the relative difference between BF and RF was smaller in regolith than in soil, 
indicating that substrate limitations constrain the effectiveness of fertilizer amendments.

Crop-Specific Responses 
Differences in growth between plant species were observed, with tomato plants showing 
substantially greater growth than basil under identical experimental conditions. This 
suggests that plant response to substrate and fertilizer type is species dependent. 
Nutrient data support this observation. BF treatments provided higher nitrate (up to 32.11 
ppm in soil and 9.66 ppm in regolith) and potassium concentrations (up to 171.48 ppm in 
soil and 152.37 ppm in regolith), which are essential for plant growth. The enhanced growth 
of tomato plants may therefore reflect higher nutrient use efficiency (NUE), particularly for 
nitrogen. 
In contrast, basil exhibited comparatively lower growth, suggesting differences in nutrient 
uptake capacity, metabolic demand, or root system development. These findings emphasize 
the importance of crop selection for optimizing growth in regolith-based systems. 
Phosphorus Measurement Limitations 
Phosphorus results showed inconsistencies, including negative values in regolith treatments 
(−5.34 ppm and −3.612 ppm), which are not physically meaningful. These values likely 
indicate concentrations below the detection limit or interference from the regolith matrix. 
In contrast, soil treatments yielded measurable phosphorus concentrations (0.4184 ppm 
for BF and 4.0653 ppm for RF), suggesting that phosphorus is more reliably retained and 
detected in soil systems. 
Future studies should refine analytical methods to improve phosphorus quantification, 
particularly in complex substrates such as regolith. 
Experimental Limitations and Future Work 
Several limitations should be considered: 
 
Short experimental duration (five weeks) limits long-term conclusions

 
Lack of root system analysis (length, thickness, nutrient uptake efficiency) future 
work. 
 
Phosphorus detection limitations in regolith 
Future work should extend the experimental timeline, include full growth cycles, and 
investigate alternative nutrient delivery strategies. 
 Conclusions 
This study demonstrates that banana-derived fertilizer is an effective organic amendment 
that enhances plant growth in both soil and regolith systems. Quantitative analysis showed 
that BF significantly increased nitrate (up to 32.11 ppm) and potassium (up to 171.48 ppm) 
concentrations compared to regular fertilizer. 
While soil remains a more efficient substrate for plant growth, regolith was able to support 
plant development when supplemented with BF. These findings suggest that organic 
fertilizers derived from waste materials, such as banana peels, can improve nutrient 
availability and partially overcome the limitations of nutrient-poor substrates. 
The results have important implications for sustainable agriculture in extraterrestrial 
environments, where in situ resource utilization and waste recycling will be essential. The 
ability of BF to enhance nutrient availability and support early plant growth suggests its 
potential application in future space missions, including the Artemis program. 
Overall, this study provides evidence that organic amendments can play a critical role in 
enabling plant growth in regolith-based systems and represents a step toward the 
development of self-sustaining agricultural systems for space exploration.
